passage:
Sunday night
Convocation photos went up. Everyone's captions have a city in them: Berlin, Bengaluru, "back to Guwahati." I have twelve browser tabs open: a job in Pune, a fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Canada, my uncle's offer at the factory. Every one of them looks right for about ten minutes. Mummy says her son can't choose a shirt, let alone a city.
Wasim called. He's joining his dad's clinic, done, decided. Part of me envied him. Part of me thought, but you'll never know what else you could have been.
It's amazing that I can go anywhere. It's also terrifying. What if I pick the wrong door and the good one closes?
Wasim said, "Pick two, give them a month each, close the rest." Closing tabs now. Hands a bit shaky.
Suraj

qa.q: How many browser tabs did Suraj have open?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Suraj have when Wasim said he had decided?
qa.a: He envied Wasim's certainty but also felt Wasim would never know what else he could have been.

qa.q: Why is Wasim's advice to pick two and give each a month useful?
qa.a: It shrinks the choice to something manageable and tests options for real, instead of freezing over twelve.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about his own settled choice?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to face so many doors, though he might sometimes wonder about paths he didn't try.

grounding: A graduate facing many careers and cities feels both excited and frozen, and a friend helps him narrow the choice.

passage: The evening bus from the district college dropped Vaibhav at the crossroads of his small town, his degree rolled up in a plastic tube. At home his sister Indu was sorting apricots on the verandah. "So, graduate sahib, what now?" she teased. He sat beside her. "That's the problem, didi. A company interview in Delhi. Teaching at the block school. Coaching for the government exam. Or staying to help Papa with the orchard." He rolled an apricot in his palm. "Every one looks good until I think about the others. Then I feel sick that I'll lose them." Indu handed him the sorting basket. "You can't eat all the apricots at once. Try one properly." He laughed, but that night he wrote the four options on a page and crossed one out.

qa.q: What was Indu sorting on the verandah?
qa.a: Apricots.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav afraid of when he says he feels sick?
qa.a: He fears that choosing one path means losing all the others, so the many options feel heavy as well as exciting.

qa.q: What small step did Vaibhav take that night, and why does it help?
qa.a: He wrote the four options down and crossed one out, making the choice smaller and easier to face.

qa.q: How does Indu see her brother's dilemma?
qa.a: She treats it lightly but kindly, teasing him and reminding him he can't try everything at once.

grounding: A new graduate back in his small town sees many possible paths and feels both excited and afraid of choosing wrongly.

passage:
Two weeks after graduation, Siddiq sat on the steps outside Thabo's flat in Johannesburg, a laptop balanced on his knees. Four tabs: a mining firm in Rustenburg, a teaching fellowship in Durban, a master's offer in Lisbon, and his aunt's shop in Cape Town.
"Look at this," he said. "Any of them could be my whole life. That's amazing, right?"
"So why do you look sick?"
"Because any of them could be the wrong whole life." He opened a fifth tab: a classmate's post from London, new job, new city, new partner. "And everyone else seems sure."
Thabo closed the laptop gently. "You've been comparing for three hours. Which one did you think about in the shower this morning?"
Siddiq was quiet. "Durban."
"Then start there. You can change later."
Siddiq laughed, shakily. It felt thrilling and terrifying at once.

qa.q: How many tabs did Siddiq have open at first?
qa.a: He had four tabs open.

qa.q: Why does Siddiq look sick even though he calls his options amazing?
qa.a: He is excited by the possibilities but dreads choosing the wrong life, especially while comparing himself with a classmate who seems sure.

qa.q: What turning point did Thabo offer, and why might it help?
qa.a: Thabo closed the laptop and asked which option Siddiq thought of in the shower, cutting through endless comparison to a first step.

qa.q: How might Thabo see Siddiq's three hours of comparing?
qa.a: Thabo seems to see it as a trap that feeds dread rather than helping, which is why the laptop gets closed.

grounding: A new graduate faces many careers and cities with both excitement and dread, caught in comparison until a friend helps him pick a first step.

passage:
The career fair filled the university sports hall with sixty stalls and a noise like a railway station. Akash, twenty-one, had a bag of brochures by eleven: a bank in Mumbai, a solar startup in Pune, a rural fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Germany.
Jahnavi found him on the bleachers. "You look like you've seen a ghost."
"I've seen sixty futures." He laughed, then didn't. "It's exciting. Every stall is a different me. But if I pick solar and the bank was right, I'll spend ten years comparing."
"You already are. You've read the bank brochure four times."
"Because Vivek got the bank, and he posts about it every day."
"Vivek is not you. Circle two you'd be curious to wake up to. Just two."
Akash took out a pen. His hand hovered, then circled solar and Odisha.

qa.q: How many stalls filled the sports hall?
qa.a: Sixty stalls filled the sports hall.

qa.q: What does Akash mean by 'Every stall is a different me'?
qa.a: He feels excited by all the possible selves but also dreads choosing wrongly and comparing forever.

qa.q: What small step did Jahnavi suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Circling just two options he'd be curious to wake up to, which narrows the choice so it doesn't freeze him.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's rereading of the bank brochure?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees it as comparison with Vivek rather than real interest, which is why Jahnavi reminds him that Vivek is not him.

grounding: A graduate at a career fair feels both excitement and dread at many possible futures, stuck comparing until a friend helps narrow the choice.
